scenes.entry_anchor: In a few evenings, Sumi wants you to dance for her guests.

You're a maiko, a geisha apprentice in Gion, Kyoto, around eighteen ninety-five. Sumi is an experienced geiko, the local name for a fully trained artist. You've watched her make a room fall quiet. Now she is offering you a small part of her evening.
Sumi is
You've watched
Now she is offering
There's one problem. In rehearsal, you keep rushing the moment when you're supposed to wait.
The musician finishes a phrase. Your arm is already moving into the next one.
Your arm
Your teacher stops you.
You'd hoped to impress the guests with how much you could do. At the moment, your teacher would settle for your doing a little less.
At the moment

In Gion Kobu, the district where you train, dance belongs to the Inoue school. Its style has been shaped by generations of women, with influences from Noh theatre and puppet performance. A held position can carry meaning. Stillness gives the viewer time to imagine what the dancer has suggested.
A held position
Knowing that doesn't make waiting easy.
As soon as the music leaves you a little space, you feel exposed. Surely everyone will think you've forgotten something. So you move, and spoil the moment you were trying to save.
So you move
Your teacher shows the passage again. This time, you watch what happens after the movement has finished.
Her attention stays in the scene. Yours has been jumping ahead to the next instruction.
Yours has
When you try again, your shoulder stays relaxed and the sleeve follows your arm. You reach the pause, hear the music continue, and remain where you are.
You reach the pause
For a moment, nothing needs rescuing.
The teacher lets you finish.
Afterwards, Hana, another learner, asks whether you were counting. She's been counting everything, including how many times she's been corrected.
She's been counting
You tell her you were listening.
She looks mildly disappointed. Counting sounded easier.

Music gives you another way into the work. During lessons, you practise the shamisen, a three-stringed instrument played with a plectrum. A note that sounded clear yesterday can become an unpleasant surprise today.
During lessons
A note
But hearing the instrument while someone sings changes what you listen for.
One older song is called Kurokami, Black Hair. It follows a woman alone with memories of someone absent. Snow gathers as the night passes. The image also suggests time leaving its marks on her.
Snow gathers
You begin to hear why a performer might linger over a phrase. The woman in the song has something to remember. Hurrying her along would change what the audience understands.
Then your own lesson resumes, and you discover that understanding a song doesn't prevent you from playing a bad note.

Later, you rehearse with Kiyo, the woman who will sing and play for your dance. She has a passage to shape, a breath to take, and a next phrase to begin. You've been treating her music as a row of signals telling you when to move.
She has a passage
You've been treating
On your second attempt, you rush again.
Kiyo stops and asks where you expected her to breathe.
You look down. You hadn't thought about it.

She plays the passage once more, without your dancing. You listen to the voice and strings together. When you stand again, the pause has a place in the music, rather than an empty space you need to fill.
You listen
When you stand again
This time, Kiyo can finish her phrase.
Sumi watches from the side of the room. She looks pleased, but she doesn't promise that the evening will be easy.
Before your own turn comes, you accompany her to a gathering at a teahouse.
Inside
The guests are talking when you enter. One man has a story about a journey. Another seems determined to tell a longer one.
Another seems
You try to look interested in both.
Sumi asks the second man whether he travelled the same route. Now the two stories have something to do with each other, and the men begin comparing their experiences.
She's found a way to include someone who was competing for attention.
When a guest asks about your dancing, you answer with the name of a piece you've been learning. He asks what happens in it.
You know the order of the movements. For a dreadful moment, that seems to be everything you know.
Sumi gives you room to answer. She doesn't immediately speak for you.

You explain the little scene as best you can. The guest asks another question, and this one is easier. By the time the conversation moves on, you've managed to say something about the work instead of merely announcing that you study it.
On the way home, Sumi asks which part was hardest.
You admit that you'd been ready to dance, but not to talk about the dance.
She laughs softly. You've given her something useful to work on tomorrow.
The next day, you describe your piece to Hana before practising it. She asks questions whenever you become vague. It's an inconvenient talent in a friend, and exactly what you need.
She asks questions

The scene you're preparing is light: a person fishing, watching the line, then responding to what might be a catch. A fan helps suggest the action. There's no river in the room. The audience has to build part of the scene in its imagination.
A fan helps
There's no river
Hana disagrees. When you hurry the waiting, she can't tell why you react afterwards.
she can't tell
You try it more slowly. The small pause you've been fighting now has a purpose. Someone is waiting for something to happen.
The small pause
Hana leans forward before you make the next movement.
That's encouraging enough to try it again.
You still want to perform the longer version, with its additional changes of direction. When Sumi first offered you a place in the evening, that was the version you imagined giving.
one transition goes wrong
You recover
Kiyo has to adjust
The next attempt
Sumi asks whether you'd rather use the shorter version you know well.
You glance at Kiyo. She's spent the rehearsal following mistakes you hoped nobody would notice.
The shorter version keeps the scene, but leaves out the passage you wanted to use to show how far you've progressed.
You ask Kiyo to play it through with you.
By the end, you've found places where you can attend to the fishing scene instead of watching for the next possible failure.
attend to the fishing scene
You tell Sumi that this is the version you want to give.
It hurts a little to say it. You'll be doing less than you hoped. But Kiyo knows what you're preparing, and Sumi can make space for that piece in the evening.
But Kiyo knows

As the evening approaches, Gion is full of reminders that performance has more than one setting. The Miyako Odori began in eighteen seventy-two in connection with Kyoto's exhibition. It gave dancers and musicians a public stage as the old capital sought new attention after the imperial court moved to Tokyo.
That larger stage still interests you. For now, the work waiting for you is close enough that every guest can see your face.
Someone helps settle your kimono before you leave. In the mirror, white makeup and carefully arranged hair make your appearance seem more composed than your thoughts.
In the mirror
You raise your arm, check the sleeve, and practise the beginning once.
Hana watches from the doorway. Before you go, she asks what you'll do if there's no fish.
She seems satisfied with that.
At the teahouse, Sumi introduces you to the company. When the same guest asks about the dance, you have an answer ready: a small fishing scene, and the uncertainty of waiting for a catch.
He smiles. At least one part of the evening already feels familiar.
As Kiyo prepares to begin, a conversation continues at the far side of the room. You look toward Sumi. She brings the speakers back into the company, then turns her attention to you.
You look toward Sumi
She brings the speakers
Kiyo begins.
and move into
At the waiting passage, you feel the old urge to hurry. Someone is watching your hands. You want to give him something more to see.
Someone is watching
But Kiyo is still singing. You stay with the moment.
A guest shifts forward, following the imagined line.
Then the music changes, and you respond.
You've reached the turn. Your shoulder stays easy. The sleeve follows.
The guest who asked
You laugh, partly from relief. For those few moments, he had been watching the fishing scene, rather than a nervous apprentice trying to remember instructions.
When you sit down, Kiyo catches your eye. She's finished her part without having to chase yours.
Later, Sumi tells you which passage still needs attention. Then she asks you to bring the same piece to another gathering.
You ask whether Kiyo will be playing.
Sumi says she will find out. You tell her you'd like to rehearse together first.
This time, she asks you when you can be ready.
The next morning, Hana wants to know whether the guests understood the fish.
Then she holds out her fan and asks you to watch her practise. At the pause, she glances toward you, anxious to move on.
